Field studies of the Red gurnard (Chelidonichthys cuculus) indicate that females reach a considerable ultimate total length of 70 cm [Li = 70 cm], a size that places this species among the larger members of the family Triglidae. The total length at which 50% of individuals are estimated to attain sexual maturity is 26.6 cm [Lp = 26.6 cm], a value derived from macroscopic examination of gonadal development in specimens collected during research trawl surveys. This notable difference between the length at puberty and the maximum recorded size underscores a protracted period of adult somatic growth following the onset of reproductive life. At a water temperature of 10.1 °C [T = 10.1 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI), calculated as the percentage of total body weight contributed by the ovary, averaged 6% [GSI = 6%]. This value likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the comparatively cool thermal regime.

Larval development in this species proceeds rapidly under warmer conditions. For eggs incubated at 20.1 °C [T = 20.1 °C], the age at hatching, marking the transition from the yolk-dependent, chorionate embryo to the prolarval stage, is approximately 9 days [ab = approximately 9 days]. This brief period from fertilization to eclosion is consistent with observations for other triglid fishes with pelagic, yolk-laden eggs of a size comparable to those of the related northern searobin, Prionotus evolans, whose egg diameters range from 1.05 to 1.25 mm. The resulting yolk-sac larva has an initial computed wet weight at birth of roughly 0.0008 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.0008 grams], a mass derived from the volumetric formula for a sphere based on an egg diameter of 1.15 mm. The transition from endogenous, yolk-dependent nutrition to first exogenous feeding occurs shortly after mouth opening, with the onset of the exotrophic stage being a critical bottleneck for larval survival and recruitment success.

Following the pelagic larval phase and subsequent settlement to a demersal habitat, juvenile Red gurnard undergo a period of rapid mass accumulation. Upon attaining the length at puberty of 26.6 cm [Lp = 26.6 cm], which corresponds to the onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation in the population, the estimated average wet weight for an individual at this physiological landmark is 176 grams [Wwp = 176 grams]. This value is derived from the empirically established length-weight relationship for the species, W = 0.00794 * L^3.05, which describes a slightly positively allometric growth pattern. The substantial size, both in length and mass, required to reach puberty suggests that a significant period of juvenile feeding and energy storage is a prerequisite for reproductive activation. The production of gametes and spawning behavior itself is a further energetic drain on the newly matured adult.

The maximum adult body mass, or asymptotic wet weight, that a female Red gurnard can attain over its lifetime is estimated to be approximately 3400 grams [Wwi = approximately 3400 grams], a value predicted by the same species-specific length-weight relationship when the ultimate total length of 70 cm [Li = 70 cm] is applied. This prolific increase in mass, from a less than one-gram juvenile to a several-kilogram spawning adult, involves the continued deposition of somatic tissue and the annual production of gonadal material. The lifespan of the Red gurnard, based on the analysis of annuli from sagittal otoliths, is documented to be 21 years in the wild at the prevailing mean annual water temperature of 10.1 °C [T = 10.1 °C], yielding a maximum recorded longevity of 21 years [am = 21 years].

Under laboratory conditions designed to reflect the thermal regime of its natural habitat, specifically a controlled water temperature of 10.1 °C [T = 10.1 °C], the rate of senescence and overall physiological decline sets the ultimate boundary for survival at approximately 21 years [am = approximately 21 years]. This period from larval eclosion to eventual natural mortality encompasses multiple spawning seasons, allowing for repeated reproductive contributions across the adult phase. In contrast, the early, thermally-sensitive egg and larval stages are accelerated at higher temperatures; for instance, the embryonic duration from fertilization to the hatching event at a temperature of 20.1 °C [T = 20.1 °C] is a mere 9 days [ab = 9 days]. This pronounced thermal sensitivity in early ontogeny suggests that inter-annual variability in sea surface temperature could directly influence recruitment strength by modulating survival through the planktonic larval phase, a key determinant of population dynamics for this commercially harvested species.
